t: Why You Should Respond Slowly To Misbehavior https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2012/06/30/why-you-should-respond-slowly-to-misbehavior/
q: There is a compulsion among teachers to react too quickly to misbehavior. As soon as it shows up on their radar, they’re on it in a flash, making judgments and decisions before fully understanding what it is.
But rushing toward the first suspicion of misbehavior or calling out in an attempt to interrupt it is like trying to stop milk as it’s being spilled. Once a rule has been broken, it’s broken.

It’s tough to keep your cool when you’re rushing to handle misbehavior. The stress and tension of thinking and moving fast on your feet can cause you to raise your voice or say something you’ll regret.
Dealing with misbehavior too quickly risks inciting students who are already in a heightened state, which all but guarantees an argumentative response.
Effective classroom management demands that you get the facts first before responding to misbehavior. Teachers who are quick to react often get it wrong, causing students to distrust them intensely.
By merely responding methodically to misbehavior, you’ll empower yourself to keep your composure, maintain control of your class, and make the right decisions with grace, clarity, and conviction.
x: Reacting instantly to misbehavior, before fully understanding it, is a compulsion that backfires and causes more stress.
Taking time before speaking or moving toward misbehavior, he argues, keeps the teacher in control no matter how severe the disruption.
Taking time before speaking or moving toward misbehavior, he argues, keeps the teacher in control no matter how severe the disruption.
Rushing to respond invites confrontation because it adds pressure to students who are already in a heightened emotional state.
Reacting too quickly blinds teachers to the actual facts, leading to inaccurate judgments and eroded student trust.
Responding methodically, rather than instantly, produces greater composure, clarity, and long-term respect from students and colleagues.

q: In one of the novel’s early scenes, we find protagonist Paul sitting in a meadow with a couple of his comrades-in-arms. Everything is pleasant about the scene — they are sitting in a circle, playing cards, laughing, talking — except for one jarring detail: they are sitting on boxes with holes in the tops with their pants around their ankles.

I will remind students that, in order to understand how this scene relates to the novel as a whole, we’ll have to look not just at what the scene says, but also what it hints at and what it doesn’t explicitly say. In teacherspeak, we’ll need to infer.

Through asking the right questions, students are led to discover that this scene is not flippant, but rather that it hints at the theme of the book: World War I was unlike anything humanity had ever seen; it devastated the men in death and life. Furthermore, this scene builds suspense at the start of the novel.

t: A Class Purpose and the Promotion of Student Flourishing
q: Essentially, I’m trying to answer the “So what?” question of my course. What is its significance to a student’s life? Why does it matter?

At the end of my courses, I want them all to have grown in their aptitudes for reading, writing, and thinking, and I also want them to have developed character. Though I still agree with this purpose statement for my students and apart from a few emphatic references to this sentence at the start of the year, I rarely mentioned it after September; few of my students could probably tell you today what the core purpose of our class was during the 2011-2012 school year.

The alternative to this is allowing Johnny to solely read books of his choosing or books that are slightly above his abilities; unfortunately, the college/career world will not make such concessions for him; inevitably, my friend Johnny will be faced with complex texts well beyond him. Lowering the standards for Johnny defeats all of my purposes as a teacher.

In other words, Graff helped me see that my students will become more comfortable in the argumentative cultures of the various academic disciplines when they see them as akin to the argumentative cultures they are already comfortable in. This coming school year, I’m going to spend the first month attempting to more fully achieve this bridging with my students, but in the past year I saw great success in this area simply by repeatedly arranging for frequent debates in our history and English classes.

So even as a beginning teacher in Baltimore, I knew I wanted my students to become more than better readers, writers, and thinkers. I knew that academically and intellectually strong people can still be horrible friends and miserable coworkers if they lack the ability to be nice or the grit to work hard.

The seven strengths — grit, zest, optimism, self-control, social intelligence, gratitude, and curiosity — were chosen from a list of 24 human virtues compiled by Peterson and Seligman. Though all 24 of the virtues are found to lead to “happy, engaged, and meaningful lives,” KIPP chooses to focus on the seven that are most closely linked with college and career success.
x: A class needs an explicit purpose that answers the 'So what?' question of its significance in students' lives, and it must be revisited all year to matter.

t: How To Use The Preview Strategy To Improve Behavior e-behavior/
q: The preview strategy is intrinsic in nature and involves a simple piquing of your students’ interest in the activities you have planned for the day.

When you’re looking over your lesson plans before school, or better yet, when you’re first creating them, search for that “one thing” in each lesson that is potentially most interesting to your students.
The most effective teachers are able to provide for their students compelling reasons why they should pay attention, why they should lean forward and care about what they’re about to learn.
Unless you have a learning environment your students enjoy and look forward to coming to every day, then there isn’t a rule or consequence in the world that is likely to help.
So look for that “one thing” in every lesson. Reignite the joy of learning for your students.
One of the great things about the preview strategy is that it will cause you to really sell what you’re teaching.
x: It is intrinsic in nature and does not rely on prizes, praise, or external rewards to capture student interest.
The method involves identifying the single most interesting element of an upcoming lesson and briefly highlighting it for students beforehand, piquing their curiosity.
Linsin frames the technique as a way to reignite joy in learning, arguing that when students look forward to lessons, misbehavior becomes far less likely.

t: How To Be Consistent With Classroom Management gement/
q: The solution is confidence, confidence in knowing that it is indeed best to follow through with your classroom management plan every single time.
To enforce your agreed-upon consequences sometimes and not others is grossly unfair to your students.
Whenever you say you’re going to do something and don’t do it, you lose a layer of respect from your students.
When your most challenging students learn that you’re not so committed to enforcing consequences, that your classroom management plan is written in pencil, they’ll smell blood in the water.
Wherever there is weak accountability or semi accountability, behavior, respect, and kindness take a nosedive.

A well-written classroom management plan, on the other hand, followed as taught, modeled, and practiced, is fair to all students and never creates resentment, friction, and hard feelings between the teacher and her students.
x: A single, objective classroom management plan applied to every student (barring documented IEP accommodations) is fairer and more effective than individualized standards.
Inconsistent enforcement is perceived by students as unfair and breeds resentment, especially toward students seen as getting special treatment.
Failing to follow through erodes teacher respect and invites more frequent testing and boundary-pushing from challenging students.
Most teachers only 'kinda-sorta' follow their classroom management plan, adjusting consequences based on mood or circumstance rather than enforcing them uniformly.
Weak accountability correlates directly with worse behavior, less learning, and greater teacher frustration and burnout.

t: Why Before School Is The Perfect Time To Build Rapport https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2012/06/09/building-rapport-with-students-before-school/
q: Because having rapport with students translates to powerful and behavior-influencing leverage—the kind of leverage that compels them to want to behave, to want to do well, and to want to please you.
Simply being with your students outside the limits of the classroom is an easy, organic way to build rapport.
The idea that yesterday’s mistakes and misbehaviors are forgotten is an important part of an overall strategy to turn around your most difficult students.
The biggest mistake teachers make when attempting to build rapport is that they try too hard. They dominate the conversation—talking at, rather than with, students.
The truth is, having a healthy, trusting, and influential rapport with students, the kind that gives your classroom management plan relevance and meaning, is primarily a function of your likeability.
Listen more than talk. Don’t try so hard. Let the conversation come to you—and then let it go where it goes.
x: Spending five minutes with students before school builds behavior-influencing rapport and leverage more efficiently than almost any in-class strategy.

Before-school interactions help prove to skeptical or difficult students that each day is a fresh start, reinforcing a core turnaround strategy.

t: Are You Sabotaging Your Own Classroom Management Success? ement-success/
q: The fact is, it doesn’t matter where you teach or who shows up on your roster, the well-behaved classroom you long for is within your grasp.
A defeatist point of view will undermine everything you do—sealing your fate to a career of frustration, disappointment, and dissatisfaction.
In order to create the class you really want, you have to believe deep down that you can—not merely as a possibility, but as a foregone conclusion that you will.
The truth is, offering excuses, even in the privacy of your own mind, is akin to giving up on your students—as well as on yourself.
By taking responsibility for everything within the four walls of your classroom, you instantly become a better, more effective teacher.
There are scores of teachers all over the world, some in the most difficult circumstances imaginable, who this very minute are enjoying the dream class they’ve always wanted.
x: A negative, defeatist attitude — not a student's background or circumstances — is the real obstacle standing between a teacher and a well-managed classroom.
Responding to a recurring reader question about disadvantaged students, Linsin argues that a negative attitude, not circumstance, is the real barrier to effective classroom management.

Making excuses based on students' home lives or neighborhoods amounts to giving up on both the students and oneself.
Teachers must take ownership of everything happening in their classroom regardless of whether they are directly responsible for a given incident.

He insists that teachers in the most difficult circumstances imaginable have achieved dream classes, and that the same is possible for any reader willing to change their thinking and commit to the process.
